POV: You're hitting the wall at mile 19 of the TCS New York City Marathon and you remember your “ultimate why.” 🥹 That’s what will motivate you to cross the finish line, right? 🏆

Science says NOPE. 🙅‍♀️ Research by NYU psychologist Emily Balcetis has shown that when things get tough, elite runners actually focus on the “how”—the next tiny, concrete step in the journey. 

We talked to her ahead of the iconic November 2 race for some evidence-backed strategy tips (with more on the study at the link in our bio). 

Special thanks to Special thanks to Julian Aske (NYU College of Arts and Science '27) of NYU's Cross Country team for starring as our model runner!

Campus Advisory Update (3:00 p.m.): Police Have Given “All Clear”

NYPD have completed their investigation of the NYU bus fleet along Broadway and given an all clear notice. Vehicular traffic on Broadway has also resumed. Entrances and exits to NYU buildings along Broadway have re-opened.

NYU bus service will resume as quickly as possible, and will follow the posted schedule: https://www.nyu.edu/life/travel-and-transportation/university-transportation/routes-and-schedules.html

Advisory Update, 2:45 p.m.: Broadway Shut Between Waverly Pl and Washington Pl While Police Investigate

Vehicular and pedestrian traffic have been temporarily shut along Broadway between Waverly Place and Washington Place, as have entrances and exits to NYU buildings in that area, while police search buses in that vicinity. 

Offices and schools should accommodate students and employees whose schedule may be affected by the suspension of NYU's transportation service and traffic disruptions.

Campus Advisory, October 23, 2:20 p.m.: NYU Bus Service Halted

A bomb threat against NYU-operated buses has been posted on an app that tracks NYU buses. All NYU bus service has been halted as a result of the threat; all passengers have been discharged.

Law enforcement has been notified, and will be searching the buses.

NYU community members should make other transportation arrangements until further notice. 

Updates: nyu.edu/alert

The November 4 elections are in the home stretch for eligible voters. 🏁 

This Saturday, October 25, is the last day to register and to request an absentee ballot in New York. And early Voting in New York City runs October 25–November 2.

NYUers can email nyuvotes@nyu.edu anytime for answers to your questions—or stop by one of our upcoming pop-up events in Bobst Library and the Kimmel Center.

Bartosz Bonczak was working at @NYU’s Center for Urban Science and Progress (CUSP) when professor of urban science and planning Constantine Kontokosta connected him with the New York Hall of Science. The museum in the Corona section of Queens was looking for a wide variety of experts to help plan a permanent exhibit for school-age learners on urban infrastructure, including sewers and subways.

Bonczak jumped at the chance to help represent how infrastructure intersects with city dwellers’ everyday lives, as well as how advances in engineering may reshape urban planning in the future. Titled “CityWorks,” the exhibition opened in May 2025, giving the museum’s 400,000 annual visitors an interactive feel for, and understanding of, the mechanisms and engineering works that allow New York, and every city, to function efficiently. 

For example, visitors to the exhibit can operate the steering wheel of a blue municipal “bus” while staring into a “windshield” that streams a vendor’s cart butting into traffic, a double-parked delivery truck, and jaywalkers.    

Read about the exhibit and its other interactive features: https://bit.ly/47g2iCM 

📷 : Photos by Tracey Friedman

text:
In early June, Tulsa Mayor Monroe Nichols announced the creation of a fund for the restoration of the city’s Greenwood neighborhood.

After hearing of the news from the mayor, historian and writer Quraysh Ali Lansana immediately began work on incorporating Nichols’ proposal into “Black Capitalism and the Struggle for Freedom in America,” the course he teaches at @NYUTulsa.

Lansana uses Greenwood as a case study in his survey of the economic struggles and successes of Black Americans. Once a thriving community known as Black Wall Street, Greenwood boasted thousands of residences as well as banks, shops, hotels, and theaters. On May 31, 1921, white residents invaded the district, killing as many as 300 Black residents while destroying thousands of homes and businesses in the worst incident of racial violence in American history.

This semester, his class will have a front-row seat for the creation of the Greenwood Trust and its potential to change the community. It will serve as a coda for the course, which traces the influence of economics, politics, and culture not only in Tulsa, but Chicago, Pittsburgh, Detroit, and Harlem. The class explores the policies of reconstruction, the influence of money, the anxiety of the Red Scare (a time of national fear about communism), and the manipulation of the law. Students are required to write response papers to class discussions, readings, and field trips to the Greenwood district and its cultural sites.

Learn more about the cool course: https://www.nyu.edu/about/news-publications/news/2025/october/cool-course--black-capitalism-and-the-struggle-for-freedom-in-am.html

text:
“We're in the middle of a science and technology revival at NYU, where the plan is to invest in over a hundred new faculty hires over the next few years,” said Juan de Pablo, the university’s inaugural executive vice president for global science and technology and NYU Tandon School of Engineering dean, at last week's NYC Quantum Summit 2025. Hosted at the Kimmel Center and organized by NYU physicist Javad Shabani, the two-day event brought together 200 leaders in this burgeoning scientific field to discuss the current state of quantum—and its potential to change our lives. 

Quantum ultimately refers to the peculiar physics of subatomic matter, which, for reasons both known and unknown, operates by a completely different set of rules compared to macroscopic, or visible, particles. Experts at the summit said that almost all advanced technology today relies on quantum mechanics, and estimated that the quantum workforce will soon need to grow by about 200,000 people. That's why NYU is investing in it—with a new master's degree and a new institute.

In his remarks, de Pablo noted that "almost a hundred years ago, in 1928, Robert Mulliken from NYU’s Department of Chemistry was the first to assign quantum numbers to the electrons in molecules." Learn more about how we're building on that legacy at the link in our bio: https://www.nyu.edu/about/news-publications/news/2025/october/top-quantum-scientists-convene-at-nyu.html

NYU students in Professor David Darts’s “Intro to Galleries and Museums of NYC” course recently spent an afternoon in Chelsea, where they powered through ten commercial galleries with new art of all kinds.

The NYU Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development course explores the different types of institutions that make up the city’s arts ecosystem. “We focus on contemporary art, which is something that New York really showcases,” Darts said. “The course provides a language to discuss art, so they can stand in front of a work and talk about it, ask questions about it, and form an opinion about it.”

While at the galleries, Darts asked each student to pick one work they would like to buy and to photograph it. Afterward, they had to answer a few questions about living with their choice, including where and how they would display it. Read more about the Cool Course: https://bit.ly/46G4IeZ

text:
Scientists are increasingly turning to AI to model future changes in the climate. However, existing approaches often lack precision, oversimplifying natural phenomena and reducing the accuracy of their predictions as a result. 

Researchers at NYU Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Center for Data Science have now developed a first-of-its-kind neural network—Samudra—that emulates the ocean in 3D. Samudra (Sanskrit for “ocean”) reproduces key ocean variables like sea surface height, ocean currents, temperature, and salinity throughout the ocean’s depth, offering a detailed look at earth’s vast waterways. And it does so 100 times faster than many existing methods and at a lower cost. 

We went straight to the source and asked Laure Zanna, a professor at Courant and the Center for Data Science, to tell us more. Read on at the link in our bio!

text:
NYU just unveiled Torch, the most powerful supercomputer in the state of New York, named for the university's logo. Torch is five times more powerful than our previous supercomputer, Greene, as well as more sustainable: Torch was recently ranked No. 40 on the Top Green 500, a global list of the most sustainable supercomputers in the world, thanks to its advanced liquid cooling system. Greene, which came online in 2020, was ranked No. 50 on the same list.

“Torch will empower NYU’s research community to achieve new heights of scientific exploration in the fields of AI, climate modeling and Alzheimer’s research, to name just a few, as they push the boundaries of innovation even further," says Stacie Bloom, NYU's Chief Research Officer & Vice Provost for Research.

We chatted with some of the researchers who will be using the supercomputer to supercharge their projects.

text:
A new way to deal with cavities could be a game-changer in oral health. Using zinc, NYU scientists are developing a treatment for tooth decay that fights bacteria, blocks pain, and avoids staining teeth—all without drilling. 

Marc Walters, professor of chemistry at NYU, has long studied silver and other elements used in medicine to carry drugs and imaging contrast agents. Several years ago, he was approached by researchers at NYU College of Dentistry seeking to better understand how silver stains teeth in order to avoid that outcome.

Walters had an idea. What if another mineral could be used that was also colorless and antimicrobial but didn’t turn teeth black? This question led him to zinc. Read about the journey and Walters' important discovery: https://bit.ly/4nu9t1a

📷 : Photos by Jonathan King

Want to get more involved? Sign up for a story exchange workshop led by Narrative 4 in the Kimmel Center on October 6 (link in bio)!

text:
NYU researchers made this. But what is it? Hint: It's not a lava lamp.

Through a series of experiments, a team of NYU scientists pinpointed some of the factors that cause icebergs to capsize, offering insights into how climate change may affect Earth’s waters.

“We learned that melting primarily happens along the wetted surface of the ice below the waterline while the ‘tip’ out of the water is almost unaffected, which eventually leaves the ice top heavy so that it loses gravitational stability in the water and rotates over,” explains NYU Courant's Leif Ristroph, the senior author of the paper. “Our study contributes fundamental knowledge about ice physics, which is a vital factor in the health of our planet and which needs to be understood to improve climate modeling and weather forecasting.”  Learn all about it at the link in our bio.

This week, five NYU scholars took us back to school on artificial intelligence—from using AI to study birds and buildings to being mindful of its biases. They shared their research with The Academic Minute on WAMC Northeast Public Radio for a weeklong look at AI at NYU:

🤖  Arthur L. Carter Journalism Institute's Meredith Broussard on biases built into AI systems: https://bit.ly/4mr4Cwe

🐦 NYU Tandon School of Engineering's David Fouey on "Skelevision," an AI vision system that identifies and measures bird bones https://bit.ly/4gxsA7T

🧠 NYU Arts & Science's Marcelo Mattar on using AI to uncover how we make decisions: https://bit.ly/4pvpFRd

🏢 NYU Robert F. Wagner Graduate School of Public Service's Daniel Neill on using machine learning to find where building issues are underreported in New York City: https://bit.ly/3W25qwI

🎒 NYU Arts & Science and NYU Center for Data Science Cristina Savin takes AI to kindergarten to train it on simple tasks before it tackles complex ones: https://bit.ly/4gHbVib

text:
We’ve all heard the saying that to better understand someone, you should try walking a mile in their shoes. But imagine being able to enter a life-sized shoe box, pluck a pair off a shelf, try them on for size, and take a stroll while listening to the original owner’s story.

NYU’s A Mile in My Shoes, in partnership with the Empathy Museum, invites all students, faculty, administrators, and staff to do just that from from now until October 15 at the Paulson Center and until October 26 at 2 MetroTech in Brooklyn. Some of the museum’s 350 previously collected stories will be available to listen to alongside new NYU entries produced by and featuring voices from the university community. 

With anecdotes from a disability advocate, a war veteran, a hospital chaplain, and more, the stories cover grief and hope, love and conflict. Visitors will select a pair of shoes and the story that goes with them, scan a QR code to listen to the personal narrative, and—if they wish—step into someone else’s shoes and walk along one of the suggested neighborhood routes.

Stories have so far been collected in several languages across 19 countries, and the exhibition has previously stopped in Denver, Milan, and Melbourne. At NYU, marking the first time the museum has collaborated with an American university, the installations will be staffed in part by students, who will assist to curate the visitor experience and answer questions. Inspired to share your story? Deepen the experience by joining a Story Exchange workshop on September 29 or October 6. Check out the details: https://bit.ly/48mBSRS

text:
AI is OK at recognizing simple images in isolation, but when asked to make sense of complex terrain—like a busy city intersection—it’s not so great. That’s a problem for self-driving car technology.

So NYU researchers are working on an algorithm to help AI systems learn from their environment, inspired by how humans and animals process cluttered scenes.

Their method, PooDLe, captures both foreground images (e.g., pedestrians crossing the street) and background images (distant cross streets) using “optical flow”—information about how pixels move between video frames. This process allows for the identification of paired regions containing the same object across time—such as a pedestrian moving from the curb to a crosswalk and continuing down a crowded street. 

Learn more: https://www.nyu.edu/about/news-publications/news/2025/september/putting-ai-vision-into-better-focus.html
